planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root seedlings in fall or early spring in average to moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; loblolly pine grows quickly on a wide range of soils and is the dominant commercial timber pine of the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain.

directions: Plant container-grown or bare-root seedlings in fall or early spring in average to moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; loblolly pine grows quickly on a wide range of soils and is the dominant commercial timber pine of the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain. Long, dark green needles in bundles of three clothe a fast-growing, straight-trunked tree that can add two or more feet of height per year on a good site, eventually reaching well over 100 feet with a broad, rounded crown at maturity, making it one of the most economically important timber and pulpwood trees in the American South. It reseeds itself readily on disturbed and cutover ground and is a familiar, defining tree of the region's forests, providing habitat and seed for a wide range of birds and mammals including favored nesting habitat for red-cockaded woodpeckers in older stands. Give it plenty of room to reach full size, since it is not a small-yard tree, and avoid planting where ice storms or hurricane-force wind could bring down large limbs near structures.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in rocky, alkaline, well-drained limestone soil in full sun; Ashe juniper is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established and needs no irrigation beyond its first year or two.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in rocky, alkaline, well-drained limestone soil in full sun; Ashe juniper is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established and needs no irrigation beyond its first year or two. Dense, scale-like, dark green foliage covers a shrubby to small tree form native to the limestone hills of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau, where it is often called 'mountain cedar' and forms extensive brakes on rocky slopes too thin-soiled for most other trees. Its winter pollen, released in massive quantities from December through February, is the primary cause of the region's notorious 'cedar fever' allergy season, a significant consideration before planting near a home; mature female trees produce small, blue, berry-like cones that are valuable winter food for cedar waxwings and other birds. Established stands provide critical nesting habitat for the endangered golden-cheeked warbler, which nests almost exclusively in old-growth Ashe juniper bark strips, making mature stands ecologically valuable despite the tree's reputation as a rangeland weed when it encroaches on grazing land.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; redberry juniper is exceptionally drought-tolerant, adapted to the caliche and limestone soils of west and central Texas rangeland.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; redberry juniper is exceptionally drought-tolerant, adapted to the caliche and limestone soils of west and central Texas rangeland. Dense, scale-like, blue-green to gray-green foliage covers a shrubby, multi-trunked small tree that produces distinctive brick-red to copper-colored, berry-like cones rather than the more typical blue-gray of most junipers, making it easy to distinguish from the similar Ashe juniper it often grows alongside. Native to the rocky plains, canyons, and mesas of west and central Texas, New Mexico, and Oklahoma, it provides valuable cover and winter food for wildlife and tolerates the region's extreme heat, drought, and thin, rocky soils with ease once established. It is considered a rangeland-encroachment concern in some grazing contexts but remains a tough, low-water landscape choice for xeriscape plantings on difficult, rocky sites.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Virginia snakeroot is a small woodland understory herb that needs the same rich, leafy shade conditions as trilliums and other spring ephemerals.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Virginia snakeroot is a small woodland understory herb that needs the same rich, leafy shade conditions as trilliums and other spring ephemerals. Slender, zigzagging stems carry heart-shaped leaves close to the forest floor, with small, curved, pipe-shaped brownish-purple flowers produced low at the base of the plant, largely hidden beneath the leaf litter and pollinated by small flies. As a member of the pipevine family, it serves as a larval host plant for pipevine swallowtail butterflies, though it is a smaller, less vigorous host than the woody pipevine (Aristolochia macrophylla) more commonly planted for that purpose. Historically valued in traditional medicine for its aromatic rhizome, it is grown today mainly as a woodland native curiosity and butterfly host plant, spreading slowly by rhizome in rich, undisturbed shade.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; slimleaf pawpaw is adapted to dry, sandy pinelands and needs sharper drainage than the common pawpaw of the eastern woodlands.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; slimleaf pawpaw is adapted to dry, sandy pinelands and needs sharper drainage than the common pawpaw of the eastern woodlands. Narrow, willow-like leaves and creamy white to pale yellow, nodding flowers set this small shrubby tree apart from the common pawpaw, and it bears small, fragrant, yellow-green fruit with the characteristic custardy pawpaw flavor, though smaller and less commonly harvested than named common pawpaw cultivars. Native to the fire-maintained sandhill and scrub habitats of Florida, Georgia, and the western Gulf coastal plain, it is well adapted to the region's characteristic dry, sandy, nutrient-poor soils and periodic natural fire, resprouting readily from its root system after top damage. It serves the same role as other pawpaws as a larval host plant for zebra swallowtail butterflies and needs little supplemental water once its extensive root system is established in sandy soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in well-drained, limestone-based upland soil in full sun to partial shade; September elm tolerates the same range of soils as other native elms and needs little care once established.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in well-drained, limestone-based upland soil in full sun to partial shade; September elm tolerates the same range of soils as other native elms and needs little care once established. Unlike every other native elm, which flowers in late winter or very early spring before leafing out, this uncommon species flowers and sets its winged seeds in September and October, giving the tree its distinctive common name and making it easy to identify in fall when its papery samaras are conspicuous against the still-green foliage. Native to scattered limestone bluffs and upland woods across the mid-South and lower Midwest, it is considered rare and local throughout its range, making cultivated plantings valuable for conserving the species' genetic diversity outside isolated wild populations. Like other American elms it is susceptible to Dutch elm disease, though reportedly to a somewhat lesser degree than American elm, and provides the same wildlife and shade value as more common elm species where it can be sourced from a specialty native nursery.
